title: First FALN Bombing Wave
body:
The Fuerzas Armadas de Liberación Nacional (FALN) announced itself on the U.S. mainland on October 26, 1974, setting off a coordinated series of bombs at symbolic government and corporate targets in New York City, including several Manhattan banks. In communiqués the clandestine group claimed responsibility and declared its aim: independence for Puerto Rico from United States colonial rule.

The wave opened what would become one of the most sustained clandestine bombing campaigns in modern U.S. history. Rooted in the long tradition of the Puerto Rican independence movement — from the Nationalist Party of the 1950s onward — the FALN framed its actions as armed resistance to colonialism rather than ordinary crime.

title: Fraunces Tavern Bombing
body:
On January 24, 1975, the FALN bombed Fraunces Tavern, a historic restaurant in Lower Manhattan, killing four people and injuring more than fifty. It was the deadliest attack of the group's campaign, and the FALN claimed responsibility in a communiqué tying the bombing to its demand for Puerto Rican independence.

The bombing shocked the public and made the FALN a national law-enforcement priority. It remains the single most controversial episode in the group's history and figured heavily in later debates over how its imprisoned members should be judged — as terrorists or as combatants in an anti-colonial struggle.

title: The Mainland Bombing Campaign
body:
Between 1974 and 1983 the FALN claimed well over a hundred bombings and incendiary attacks, concentrated in New York and Chicago but extending to Washington, D.C., and other cities. Targets included banks, corporate headquarters, government buildings, and military and political offices — chosen as symbols of U.S. colonial and capitalist power.

The scale and persistence of the campaign made the FALN the most prominent Puerto Rican clandestine organization operating on the mainland, and it drew a massive federal response. The group deliberately used property destruction and telephoned warnings in many actions, though several attacks — above all Fraunces Tavern — caused deaths and injuries.

title: Cook County Building Bombing
body:
In 1977 the FALN carried out a major bombing at the Cook County Building in Chicago, one of the most significant of its actions outside New York. Chicago, with its large Puerto Rican community, was a central base for the organization, and the attack underscored that the FALN's campaign was national in scope.

The Chicago bombings helped focus federal investigators on the city's Puerto Rican independence networks — an investigation that would culminate in the 1980 Evanston arrests that broke much of the FALN's mainland structure.

title: William Morales Explosion & Escape
body:
In 1978 William Morales, a leading FALN bomb-maker, was gravely injured when explosives detonated prematurely at a bomb factory in Queens, New York; he lost most of both hands and part of his face. Arrested and convicted, he became one of the most closely watched FALN prisoners.

In 1979 Morales made a dramatic escape from the prison ward of Bellevue Hospital and went underground. He eventually reached Mexico and later Cuba, which gave him refuge — placing him among the Puerto Rican independence figures living in exile beyond the reach of U.S. prosecution.

title: Evanston Arrests
body:
In April 1980, eleven FALN members were arrested in Evanston, Illinois, effectively decapitating the organization's mainland network. The arrests followed years of federal investigation into the Chicago-based independence underground.

The captured members refused to recognize the authority of the U.S. court, declaring themselves prisoners of war in an anti-colonial struggle and declining to mount a conventional legal defense. Their stance framed the prosecutions that followed and shaped the long campaign for their release.

title: Seditious-Conspiracy Convictions
body:
In the early 1980s, following the Evanston arrests, several FALN members were tried in federal court and convicted of seditious conspiracy — conspiring to oppose U.S. authority over Puerto Rico by force — along with weapons and other charges. Many received sentences of decades, far longer than those typical for the underlying offenses.

The use of the rarely-invoked seditious-conspiracy statute, and the length of the sentences, became central to the argument that the FALN prisoners were being punished for their political beliefs and their commitment to independence. Their cases joined the long lineage of Puerto Rican nationalists imprisoned under the same charge, stretching back to Pedro Albizu Campos in the 1930s.

title: Oscar López Rivera’s Imprisonment
body:
Oscar López Rivera, a Chicago community organizer and Vietnam veteran, was arrested in 1981 and convicted of seditious conspiracy for his role in the FALN. Sentenced to 55 years — with additional time added later — he became the best-known and longest-held of the Puerto Rican independence prisoners.

Over more than three decades his case became an international cause, drawing support from across the Puerto Rican political spectrum, Nobel laureates, and religious leaders. In January 2017 President Barack Obama commuted his sentence, and he was released that May, greeted as a hero on his return to Puerto Rico.

title: Clinton Clemency Controversy
body:
In August 1999, President Bill Clinton offered clemency to sixteen imprisoned FALN and Puerto Rican independence members, on the condition that they renounce violence. Most accepted and were released; the offer reflected years of lobbying by Puerto Rican community and religious leaders who argued the prisoners' sentences were grossly disproportionate.

The clemency ignited a major political controversy. Congress condemned it in overwhelming votes, critics accused the administration of political motives, and it became entangled in debates over Hillary Clinton's 2000 Senate campaign. It remains one of the most contested uses of the clemency power in modern U.S. history.

title: Continuing Political-Prisoner Campaigns
body:
From the 1980s through the 2010s, the FALN cases sat at the center of Puerto Rican independence and prisoner-support organizing. Campaigns for the release of Oscar López Rivera, Carlos Alberto Torres, Haydée Beltrán, and others framed them as political prisoners of a colonial relationship and became a rare point of unity across Puerto Rican politics.

The 1999 clemencies, the 2010 release of Carlos Alberto Torres, and the 2017 commutation of Oscar López Rivera were treated as major victories by that movement. The FALN prisoners' decades of incarceration — and the organizing around them — remain a defining chapter in the modern history of the Puerto Rican independence struggle.
